entries.title: D.C. General Election Guide: What to Know Before Nov. 3
entries.summary: On the heels of a crowded June primary, voters still have plenty left to decide.
entries.content:
On the heels of a crowded June primary, D.C. voters might assume the city’s biggest political decisions are already in the books.

With Democrats holding a decisive registration advantage across the District, nominees Janeese Lewis George for mayor and Robert White for congressional delegate enter the Nov. 3 election as heavy favorites. Yet even frontrunners facing nominal competition say they are taking nothing for granted, routinely reminding supporters that they must still win the general election to secure victory.

The main event is the fight for two available at-large council seats.

That contest will work differently this year thanks to the general-election debut of ranked-choice voting — a structural shift that fundamentally alters how ballots are cast and counted.

Add a citywide measure on restaurant menus to the mix, and D.C. voters still have plenty left to decide.

Here is your guide to what’s on the Nov. 3 ballot, how the new math functions and what you need to know before marking your grid.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The At-Large Race and the New Math

The pick-two era is officially over. District voters have long been able to make two selections on their ballot for the two open at-large D.C. council seats. Under the city’s new ranked-choice voting system, voters now face a grid prompting them to rank candidates from first to fifth choice.

This shift has created a unique mathematical quirk in the general election.

To determine the two winners, election officials eliminate candidates with the lowest vote totals round by round until two remain. But because each ballot carries only one active vote at a time, a ballot locked on a winning frontrunner stays frozen — meaning your secondary rankings are never used to help select a second winner.

The dynamic stems from the District’s 1973 Home Rule Act, which reserves two of the council’s four at-large seats for non-majority party members. Combining those two seats into a single ranked race means a vote locked on a frontrunner swallows down-ballot influence for the second seat.

In deep-blue Washington, Democratic nominee Oye Owolewa is expected to draw a significant share of first-choice rankings. But Democrats whose votes stay locked with Owolewa effectively surrender their say in deciding which candidate claims the reserved non-majority seat.

That reality has altered traditional campaign strategies.

Independent incumbent Elissa Silverman — who won a June special election to fill the seat vacated by Kenyan McDuffie — has urged her supporters to rank her number one, explicitly warning that ranking a Democrat first impacts her chances.

Owolewa is countering by asking Democrats to lock in his victory as their top pick. Meanwhile, Republican Darrell Green and Statehood Green candidate Darryl Moch are competing for those same top-tier rankings in hopes of pulling off an upset.

Confusion caused by this change has been compounded by delays in voter education materials from the D.C. Board of Elections, which told The Washington Sun it faced procurement delays at the start of the fiscal year.

Janeese Lewis George (7619x5080, AR: 1.50)
The Top of the Ticket

Other races on the general election ballot follow more traditional dynamics. In the mayoral contest, Lewis George is heavily favored to succeed retiring Mayor Muriel Bowser. She faces Independent Rhonda Hamilton and Statehood Green candidate Robert L. Gross.

In the race to succeed Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as D.C.’s nonvoting voice in Congress, White faces Republican Denise Rosado and Statehood Green candidate Kymone Freeman.

Further down the ballot, two Democratic incumbents in citywide seats are seeking another term: Council Chairman Phil Mendelson faces Republican challenger Abi-Ananiah Prudent, while Attorney General Brian Schwalb defends his seat against Republican Manuel Rivera.

In the ward-level council races, three Democratic incumbents are defending their seats alongside one open-seat race:

  • Ward 1: Democratic nominee Aparna Raj faces Republican Jett James Jasper, independent Ryan Prince and Statehood Green candidate Jude Crannitch. 
  • Ward 3: Incumbent Matthew Frumin is running unopposed. 
  • Ward 5: Incumbent Zachary Parker faces Republican Jeffrey Kihien-Palza and Statehood Green candidate Joyce Robinson-Paul. 
  • Ward 6: Three-term incumbent Charles Allen faces Republican Jorge Rice
Voters will also weigh in on the city’s nonvoting shadow U.S. senator and representative seats, as well as several distinct ward-level seats on the State Board of Education.

A Ballot Measure on Foie Gras

Voters will also decide on Initiative No. 86, officially titled the Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026. A “yes” vote supports banning the force-feeding of poultry to produce foie gras and prohibits sale or distribution of those products in the District.

How and When to Vote 

Ballots were mailed to all registered D.C. voters in late September. You can return yours by mail — as long as it is postmarked by Election Day — or drop it into one of the city’s secure 24/7 ballot drop boxes.

  • Early Voting: Runs daily from Monday, Oct. 26 through Sunday, Nov. 1 between 8:30 a.m. and 7 p.m.
  • Election Day: Vote centers are open Tuesday, Nov. 3 from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
  • Same-Day Registration: Available at any early voting center or Election Day polling place with proof of D.C. residence. 
Polling locations and drop box sites can be found on the D.C. Board of Elections website.

entries.title: Ukrainian Defense Tech Companies Pitch U.S. Partnerships Despite Political Turmoil
entries.summary: As relations between the countries hit another rough patch, the firms say they can be the bridge while helping both militaries evolve.
entries.content:
Despite freshly strained relations between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian defense tech companies are courting partnerships with U.S. manufacturers, investors and the Pentagon. The firms are betting that their battlefield-tested weapons could help shore up the countries’ shaky security partnership.

“The deeper we have integration of the industries, the better we are on the political level,” said Roman Tkachenko, co-founder of Tencore, a Ukrainian manufacturer of uncrewed ground vehicles.

Tkachenko was among representatives of 17 Ukrainian defense technology companies exhibiting quadcopters of various sizes, signal jammers and uncrewed ground vehicles at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington last week. It was the conference’s first dedicated Ukraine pavilion.

The push reflects Ukraine’s growing ambitions to become a supplier of military technology rather than simply a recipient of American aid. Kyiv has eased weapons export restrictions, sought joint drone production with the U.S. and discussed a deal in which the Pentagon would purchase Ukrainian-made drones that the two countries would co-produce.

But the relationship hit another rough patch in recent days.

Trump announced a proposed deal this month to import Russian diesel, potentially providing billions of dollars to Russia’s economy. He also demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, strikes that have damaged Moscow’s energy industry and become an important part of Kyiv’s war effort.

Trump subsequently announced an energy ceasefire, but neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed agreeing to the terms, and Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s infrastructure.

The tensions deepened Wednesday when Ukraine discovered new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink satellite terminals, prompting Ukrainian officials to suspect that Trump had ordered the limitations.

John Roberts, an American advising Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, said the uncertainty surrounding U.S. military supplies has forced Ukrainian commanders to scramble their battlefield plans.

“We have to fight with what we have, and sometimes we’re told we don’t have as much stuff coming next week,” Roberts said. “When we do our forecast, it means we have to change operations.”

That’s also made Ukraine more determined to reduce its dependence on foreign military aid, Roberts said.

“Ukrainians want to be self-sufficient,” he said.

Tkachenko’s company is seeking American manufacturing partners after establishing a joint venture with Germany’s Quantum Systems and another partnership in Finland. Tencore plans to produce 2,000 ground vehicles through the German partnership over the coming year.

“I cannot tell the politicians what to do,” Tkachenko said. “But what I can do — actually, I can do my job, and I hope that my job will help to make the connection between the countries stronger.”

Tkachenko said nearly 6,000 of his company’s uncrewed ground vehicles have been deployed along Ukraine’s front lines, transporting ammunition and supplies through areas too risky to send soldiers.

Tencore has repeatedly updated its vehicles based on feedback from those troops, the type of rapid adaptation the Pentagon says it wants to achieve.

American manufacturers remain years away from matching Ukraine's drone production, which is expected to reach 6 million to 7 million small attack drones this year.

The Pentagon is seeking to rapidly fill that gap through its $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program, which has already attracted Ukrainian manufacturers. The program ordered 2,000 drones from Ukrainian Defense Drones, the American partner of Ukrainian manufacturer F-Drones.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has also announced plans for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command and is pressing Congress to approve $50 billion for drones as part of a broader $350 billion defense spending package.

But converting Ukraine’s battlefield-tested weapons into products the Pentagon can buy is a challenge. Federal restrictions on the U.S. military’s use of Chinese-made drones and components — enshrined in the National Defense Authorization Act — complicate Ukrainian manufacturers’ efforts to enter the American market because many rely heavily on Chinese suppliers.

“We've learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can't use everything that's in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it,” Hegseth said on stage at the AUSA conference.

Ukrainian manufacturers at the conference told The Washington Sun that they are developing versions of their weapons that meet American requirements, though replacing Chinese parts could make them more expensive and harder to produce at scale.

David Hensley, co-founder of Fenicks Group, the American company that organized AUSA’s Ukraine pavilion, said the companies his firm represents offer export models without Chinese components.

“They're all NDAA compliant,” Hensley said, adding that Ukrainian weapons are still cheaper than American products, despite the cost of replacing Chinese parts.

Bohdan Shtylyk, head of exports at Ukrainian drone manufacturer Stellarion, said eliminating Chinese components is possible but difficult because alternative suppliers cannot always meet the industry's production needs.

“Not every factory can match that pace,” Shtylyk said.

He said Stellarion, which produces tens of thousands of drones each month, is investing heavily in versions designed to meet U.S. requirements.

Meta Bureau, another Ukrainian company, is preparing to compete for Pentagon business with a version of its SkyKnight reusable bomber drone that replaces Chinese-made components with alternatives that meet American requirements.

Yuri Hundych, the company’s chief commercial officer, said American companies at AUSA offered the company motors, software and other technologies for its drones.

The company was invited to enter SkyKnight in a Defense Department competition next month at Michigan’s Camp Grayling, where manufacturers will demonstrate systems for possible U.S. military purchase.

Ukraine, he predicted, will remain dependent on Chinese parts as long as they are cheaper. But he said he hopes allies can expand non-Chinese supply chains enough that alternative parts are comparably priced.

“Our conflict is going into its fifth year, and budgets are limited,” he said. “You need to count every penny and give our army and our soldiers these solutions as cheaply as possible and still try to [maintain] a high level of quality.”

Still, Maj. Gen. Duane Miller, a former deputy commanding general of Security Assistance Group-Ukraine, said the Pentagon has a lot to learn from the close relationships between Ukrainian companies that make weapons and the troops that use them.

That relationship allows Ukrainian manufacturers to regularly update their equipment based on battlefield experience, he said, comparing it to commercial smartphone software. By contrast, he said, the U.S. military has traditionally bought equipment, trained soldiers to use it and moved on.

“You can’t make changes in weeks and months. You’re going to have to do this in hours and days,” he said. “The enemy is constantly adapting. What I fear is that we’re not going to learn quickly enough.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 8
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a specialist from Friendship Collegiate and a hard-hitting safety from C.H. Flowers.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This group of high school football standouts got the job done on offense, defense and special teams. Here are five players who excelled in Week 8:

King Antoine, Junior, Linebacker, St. John’s

Antoine shined on defense for the Cadets, who allowed just seven points in a 38-7 win over Good Counsel on Friday in Olney. With the junior linebacker leading the charge, St. John’s nabbed three pick-sixes on a rainy night. Antoine also contributed on offense, coming in to spell senior Da’Jon Talley-Rhodes at running back late in the second half and muscling his way through several Falcons defenders for an impressive rushing score.

“He made big plays for us on both sides of the ball,” coach Terrence Byrd said. “He was a major spark for the team.”

Jedidiah Cook, Senior, Athlete, Friendship Collegiate

Cook made his mark on special teams for the Knights, who earned a dominant victory over KIPP. Cook took the opening kickoff 96 yards for a touchdown to give Friendship Collegiate an immediate jolt in what would be a 54-0 win.

Later in the game, Cook fielded a Panthers punt and sprinted to his right. With no opening in sight, he bounced back left, found a crease and took off for another impressive touchdown. The senior had another long punt return ruled down at the 1-yard line.

Cavare Durandisse, Junior, Athlete, C.H. Flowers

The Jaguars leaned heavily on their defense in a Saturday afternoon slugfest against Prince George’s County rival Oxon Hill. Flowers produced a late defensive stand and held the Clippers to just 12 points in a 14-12 victory. Flowers is now 5-1 under first-year coach Frederick Groves.

Durandisse picked up six solo tackles at safety, including several hard hits that created incompletions. The do-it-all junior, who also plays both running back and slot receiver for the Jaguars, accumulated 126 all-purpose yards and a touchdown on offense.

Collin Henriques, Junior, Wide Receiver, Oakton

Henriques couldn’t be stopped Friday against Westfield. The junior wide receiver scored a touchdown nearly every time he touched the ball in a 35-20 win against the Bulldogs. Henriques pulled in five catches for 180 yards and four touchdowns at wide receiver and added 80 kick return yards on special teams.

With the win, Oakton moved to 7-0 for the first time since 2011 and clinched a Virginia Class 6 playoff berth. The win also snapped the program’s 14-year drought against Westfield.

Caleb Smallwood, Junior, Running Back, Magruder

Smallwood ran for 295 yards and three touchdowns for the Colonels, who needed every yard from their bell-cow back in a thrilling comeback victory over Kennedy on Thursday. In a 50-38 win, Magruder scored 22 points in the fourth quarter. Smallwood also played defense in the second half — he forced and recovered a fumble late in the fourth quarter to help seal the victory.

Between Smallwood and junior Nico Gilliam, the Colonels ran for 400-plus yards and six touchdowns on the evening.

“When we saw on film that Kennedy really liked to blitz, and our offense is a zone RPO scheme, we told our offensive line that they’re going to be bringing six to eight guys every single play,” Magruder coach Ray Fowle said. “Every single play, every single gap, win your assignment. … We've got two guys that can go to the house.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Let Us Be Your (Voter) Guide
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 19, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The Sun’s 2026 voter guide, Howard homecoming and Trump’s plans for East Potomac.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. There's a frosty start and the breeze is brisk but sunny afternoon 60s are spectacular. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

With ballots landing in mailboxes across the District, the Nov. 3 general election is officially underway.

Those who followed June’s crowded primary might expect a predictable fall. Top Democratic nominees like Janeese Lewis George for mayor and Robert White for Congressional delegate enter as heavy favorites. From new ranked-choice math to a citywide ballot measure, there is still plenty for voters left to figure out.

To help you sort through your ballot before filling in those bubbles, The Washington Sun has published its 2026 General Election Voter Guide. It breaks down every contest on the fall ballot, including a mechanical quirk in the at-large race that has caused front-running candidates to adjust their traditional campaign pitches.

The guide also includes rundowns on ward-level council contests, the proposed citywide ban on foie gras and essential details on early voting centers and drop box locations.





DEEP DIVE

Mixed feelings at The Mecca: There was a lot to celebrate over the weekend during Howard’s homecoming festivities, including a win for the football team over Morehouse. But looming in the background was the stress of a fraught period for the university and real concern about the future of the school.

After Howard made headlines by unenrolling hundreds of students this summer and offering buyouts to eligible faculty members, interim president Dr. Wayne Frederick said Friday in a “state of the university” address that more changes must be made. The university is anticipating at least 45,000 applications for a 2027–2028 freshman class with 2,200 spots. Frederick said the university must reconsider offering aid packages to students from high-income households.

“One hundred percent of students who enroll at Howard their freshman year get some type of aid from us,” he said. “That has to stop. That is going to stop.”

The school kicked off its search for a new president last month, and several students told The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad they want a leader that can handle financial issues. “I would want to see better financial asset management,” freshman Elijah Bartholomew said.

Howard alum Patrice Simpson said while she understood the concern around enrollment and incoming classes, the school needed to reinvest in enrolled students. “When you come to [Howard], you should leave with your degree,” she said.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Trump Golf Course AP - 26285714852216 (6899x4599, AR: 1.50)
President Donald Trump confirmed his much-discussed plans to build a “world championship” golf course at East Potomac Park, with renovations starting Nov. 15 and lasting through early 2028, despite an ongoing lawsuit, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

The finished course will be open to the public and create “many jobs,” the president wrote on Truth Social. The post, which did not include any mention of costs, was accompanied by a rendering of an 18-hole golf course that covers the length of East Potomac, including the Hains Point recreational area.

The announcement comes just days after a federal judge ordered a halt to tree-cutting at the golf course until next week. On Friday night, Justice Department lawyers asked for U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes to be removed from the case because she has shown “open hostility” toward the government, The Sun’s Michelle Del Rey reports.

D.C.’s likely next mayor, Lewis George, urged the council to delay advancing a bill that would legalize passenger service in self-driving cars, largely because of job loss concerns for rideshare and taxicab drivers, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle and Zara report. The bill’s author, Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, said his plans to move it forward are unchanged.

D.C.’s Department of Motor Vehicles reissued roughly 1,600 licenses and ID cards after the agency found printing defects its vendor made following a recent quality control review, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. A resident flagged the issue on Reddit with aphoto of a letter from the D.C. DMV. It said the printing defect “may cause questions regarding the validity of your credential when presented for identification purposes” and that the department fixed the issue at the vendor’s expense.

D.C. is cracking down on unsafe electric scooter and bike riders amid an uptick in traffic fatalities across the city, Martin and Kendall Staton report.

As D.C. looks to gain control of the D.C. Armory as part of the RFK stadium redevelopment, the D.C. Preservation League has nominated the site for placement on the National Register of Historic Places in an effort to protect the building’s exterior, the Washington Business Journal reports.

John Czwartacki spent decades as a Republican political communicator. Since his multiple sclerosis diagnosis forced him to retire, he’s found a new voice through painting, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington writes.





FROM VIRGINIA

New documents indicate that Trump has dropped his plans for a military complex to be attached to his proposed triumphal arch, Michelle reports.





TRIVIA


Where did the sculpture known as "The Awakening" go after it was moved from Hains Point in 2008?

  1. The Wharf
  2. Old Town Alexandria
  3. National Harbor
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

At long last, the Spirit picked up a big win at home. After dropping five of six at Audi Field, Washington earned a marquee win on Saturday, topping Gotham FC, 1-0, in D.C. Lucia Di Guglielmo’s 70th-minute goal, her first for the Spirit, made the difference against the league leaders, Nicky Wolcott writes for The Sun.

“Doing it here at home with your people against a great opponent … I think it’s huge,” coach Adrián González said. “Everyone deserves to have a game like this — the players, the team, staff, fans.”

The Commanders are in primetime tonight, facing the 49ers on Monday Night Football. But before Washington’s players could begin preparing for a trip to San Francisco, they first had to move past last week’s tie with the Giants. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson polled a few Commanders on what they did to turn the page on a deeply frustrating Sunday. Their antidotes included everything from rom-coms to pumpkin picking.

What to Watch Today

NFL: Commanders at 49ers, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Marked Safe (For Now)
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Trump’s response to the Susie Wiles talk. A post-midterms student debt squeeze. The Republican pitch that may have fallen flat in Nevada. Ukrainian defense firms’ Washington strategy. And: Teeing up this week’s fiery fairway fight.

THE LATEST

Someone has job security: It’s just over two weeks until the consequential midterms, and White House officials have a problem. Bruising headlines continue to mount over the self-dealings of people either inside the administration or close to it, buttressed by Americans' growing concern over government corruption and skyrocketing prices. After the disastrous, five-day tenure of Katie Zacharia, the White House is once again without a press secretary. The nearly iron-tight group of aides surrounding Donald Trump, who for the most part avoided the type of infighting that defined the president’s first term, seem like they’re starting to crack.

But it was the storyline that chief of staff Susie Wiles was on the chopping block that stirred Trump, according to a source familiar with his reaction. The president, the source said, told a group of aides effectively: If she goes, I go.

It’s a helluva vote of confidence for his embattled chief of staff, who has been a target for those unhappy with the direction of the White House after a series of tough weeks. But Trump is being advised by outside allies not to worry about any staffing shakeups until after the midterm elections, two sources familiar with the conversations told The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright. It’s unclear if he’ll heed the advice, as he’s openly questioned in phone conversations whether his political team is up to the moment. But the message delivered to him was, simply put: “Let’s focus on what we have to do now.”

Wiles’ supporters say that last week's palace intrigue-fueled rollercoaster has only emboldened her position. Not only has the president publicly defended Wiles repeatedly over the weekend, they say, but the press secretary’s exit is another proof point. The decision to hire Zacharia was ultimately Trump's.

Last week “shows that White House system works,” said one source close to the president and supportive of Wiles. That’s a system that Wiles put together. “And it weakens those fighting against her.” Put more bluntly by another Wiles confidant about her adversaries: “They picked the wrong fight.”

The White House pushed back on any divisions. “The anonymous sources peddling this fake nonsense are self-serving opportunists focused on themselves,” White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in a statement. “The team is united and focused on President Trump, delivering his America First agenda, and winning the midterms.”

More: Trump Appears to Have Dropped the ‘Military Complex’ Justification for His Arch • Zelenskyy Warns That Trump Waiving Russian Sanctions Is ‘Strengthening Putin’s War’ • WSJ: Putin Floats a Summit With Trump and Xi to Discuss Ukraine Deal


FROM TREASURY 


Eyes emoji scoop: The Trump administration is moving forward on plans to impose financial penalties on Americans in default on their federal student loans and hire private debt collectors to go after them, The Sun’s Jeff Stein and Kadia Goba report. But the plans are unlikely to be announced until after the midterms.

Treasury Department officials expressed concerns last year that too aggressively pursuing these measures could hurt low-income borrowers and that scores of Trump supporters would be seriously affected by going after the wages and benefits of workers who are, in many cases, struggling to hold onto their jobs. Their message: “This is not who you think it is. The demographics are not good for us,” one source said.

FROM NEVADA


The no tax on tips flop? Once expected to be a key part of the Republican sales pitch in the midterms, Trump’s signature populist tax scheme isn’t the winning bet Republicans had hoped for in Las Vegas, home of one of the nation’s largest tip-based economies. The Sun’s Christa Dutton reports from Democratic Rep. Susie Lee’s reelection bid in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, where MAGA Inc. recently pulled its support from Republican Marty O’Donnell after the no-tax-on-tips message didn’t move voters as much as the GOP hoped.

FROM THE PENTAGON


Ukrainian defense firms vs. shifting foreign policy: At the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington last week, Ukrainian defense firms had their first dedicated pavilion — part of an effort to sell their drone and other tech to the U.S. military. The Sun’s Joe Gould and Hamed Ahmadi report on the political and practical challenges facing these firms. Recent White House pressure on Ukrainian battlefield tactics and the firms’ reliance on Chinese parts are making building this new market difficult.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Teed up and teed off: Trump announced a Nov. 15 construction start date for his much-discussed redevelopment project at D.C.’s East Potomac Park golf course, despite an ongoing lawsuit aimed at halting the overhaul, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin and Zara Norman report. The surprise declaration prompted federal Judge Ana C. Reyes — who also denied the government’s motion that she recuse herself — to demand answers from the Trump administration. Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. doubled down and argued that the court shouldn’t even be able to take up the case because the plans aren’t final — and the court has no say anyway.

“Just as a decision to redesign all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum would not be

agency action, neither would a decision to redesign a golf course, or to trim trees, replace fences, expand the fairways, or mow the lawn,” Woodward wrote.

The rare weekend court saga plays up a hearing today where Reyes has demanded

National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron and deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department Gregory Wischer be prepared to testify.



More: DHS Punts Decision to End Deportation Protections for Immigrants From Ukraine and Sudan • Homan Says the Trump Administration Has a ‘Strong Case’ Against Rep. Ilhan Omar • DOGE Disruptions Upended $112 Million Epidemiology Contract





NOT US

  • Two weeks from Election Day, Texas Republicans start finger-pointing ahead of potential losses, by Natasha Korecki and Alexandra Marquez for NBC News
  • Trump Promoted Suspiciously Cheap Gas Stations. Here’s What He Didn’t Tell You. By Kathy Gilsinan and James Bikales for Politico
  • He Joined the Military. They Reported His Wife To Ice. By Nick Miroff and Nancy A. Youssef for The Atlantic




WEEK AHEAD

Today

Trump holds a campaign rally in Kansas.

JD Vance visits North Carolina.

Federal court hearing in the East Potomac golf course case.

Tuesday

Bill Clinton campaigns for Florida Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly.

Trump holds a campaign rally in North Carolina.

Wednesday

Trump holds a campaign rally in South Carolina.

Gubernatorial debates in Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Senate debates in Michigan and Kansas.

Pennsylvania 7th Congressional District debate.

Thursday

Trump holds a campaign rally in Iowa.

Friday

Trump holds a rally in Fort Myers, Florida.

Saturday

Barack Obama campaigns for Democratic candidates in Ohio.

entries.title: Trump Aides Are Getting Ready to Penalize Defaulting Student Loan Borrowers
entries.summary: Treasury officials are seeking ways to minimize the impact on vulnerable borrowers.
entries.content:
Trump administration officials are preparing to impose financial penalties on millions of Americans in default on their federal student loans next year, according to five sources familiar with the matter.

The Treasury Department is moving forward with plans to hire private debt collectors, three of the sources said, possibly as soon as November. The sources said those plans are unlikely to be announced before the midterm elections.

The planning — which has not been previously reported — shows the administration gearing up to move forward with a policy it previously put on hold out of concern for the potential consequences for the nearly 10 million borrowers in default.

The administration has grappled with internal divisions between federal agencies over how to manage the government’s $1.7 trillion student loan portfolio. Last year, the White House Office of Management and Budget began assisting the Education Department in preparing to seize federal benefits and wages from defaulted borrowers, the sources said. Treasury Department officials blocked that effort, expressing concern about the economic costs of taking punitive measures against workers.

Since then, Treasury officials have unveiled a new online portal that makes it easier for students to understand what they owe and how to pay in hopes of avoiding further penalties. The administration’s preference remains to get borrowers into a plan where they will make voluntary payments.

While some administration officials are pushing to garnish benefits and wages for the current tax year — meaning for the tax year deadline of April 15, 2027 — sources cautioned that it may be delayed again, as the administration wants to ensure that Treasury’s new Defaulted Loans Support Center is working.

“They wanted to make sure the infrastructure is in place to receive borrowers trying to get out of default — you can bet a lot of people will get calls from borrowers saying, ‘What’s going on? How do I make sure this won’t happen again?,’” one of the sources said. “It’s definitely something they’re thinking about. It would be politically insane to do this before the midterms — but 2027 probably makes a little more sense to give Treasury time to get contracts signed, up and running.”

OMB and Treasury declined to comment. The Education Department said in a statement: “We don’t respond to fishing expeditions.”

The government has two primary programs to claw back money from defaulting borrowers. One would seize expected payments when they follow taxes, such as expected tax refunds, Social Security payments, or the earned income tax credit and child tax credit. The other would garnish wages by requiring workers' employers to fork over what they owe to the government instead.

Last year, Treasury officials expressed concerns that too aggressively pursuing these measures could hurt low-income borrowers, two sources said. Staff also said they pointed out to senior Treasury officials that scores of Trump supporters would be seriously hurt by going after the wages and benefits of workers who are in many cases struggling to hold onto their jobs. Their message was, “This is not who you think it is. The demographics are not good for us,” one source said.

Matt Chingos, a Treasury official who worked as a Senate Republican staffer, has been spearheading the effort to both restart collections while mitigating potential consequences.

Treasury’s concerns demonstrate the practical difficulty of Republicans’ opposition to student debt forgiveness.

Treasury’s push last year to postpone collections has cost taxpayers about $5 billion so far, according to Marc Goldwein, senior vice president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan think tank. That amount grows the longer the administration waits.

“They’ve done the same thing they criticized Biden for — we shouldn’t be canceling student debt for people who just don’t want to pay,” Goldwein said. “It doesn’t create a sustainable student loan program.”

Preston Cooper, a student debt expert at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right think tank, has argued that restarting debt collection should involve a widespread effort from multiple government agencies to try to get borrowers from defaulting in the first place. He has suggested measures including pushing colleges to spread the message, distributing warnings at a "large scale" and having the Education Department send out warnings.

“We should allow them to do the right thing and not hit them with excessive fees and allow them to rehabilitate and get on an affordable repayment plan,” Cooper said. “Somewhere between treating them all as deadbeats and forgiving all the loans is probably the right solution.”

Advocates for student borrowers see efforts to punish defaulting debtors as a cruel way to extract money from borrowers who are already struggling with high inflation and rising debt burdens.

They also see the Trump administration engaging in political opportunism in delaying an announcement on their plans until after the upcoming midterm elections.

The Treasury Department may not even have the adequate data necessary to certify the debts for collection, which is a legal prerequisite for carrying them out, according to Michael Pierce, the executive director of Protect Borrowers, an advocacy organization.

The freeze on student loan payments and interest, initially implemented under Trump’s first term, also changed expectations for millions of borrowers.

“Restarting debt collection the moment any political accountability has passed just shows how little interest Trump has in helping working families stay afloat,” Pierce said. “What comes next will be a catastrophe for families across the country — seized tax refunds, garnished wages, and even less money to put food on the table or make rent.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein, Kadia Goba

entries.title: The Race That Could Test the Power of Trump’s No Tax on Tips
entries.summary: How persuasive no taxes on tips will ultimately be in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District is up to how each party frames it and the reconciliation package it was tucked into.
entries.content:
LAS VEGAS — Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, a district President Donald Trump won in 2024 where tourism fuels the economy and tips create livelihoods, is perhaps one of the best places for a Republican to run on their party’s no-tax-on-tips legislation.

With just a few weeks left until Election Day, the race seems to have shifted in Democrats’ favor. Rep. Susie Lee, the Democratic incumbent, is running in Nevada’s most competitive House district against Republican opponent Marty O’Donnell by making the case that while she supports no tax on tips, the rest of the provisions in Republicans’ 2025 reconciliation bill, which put the policy in effect, have translated to pain for constituents.

“When people are feeling the pressure economically, the first thing they drop off of their list of things they're going to do is their trip to Las Vegas,” Lee said in an interview with The Washington Sun before a community event. “That has ripple effects in our economy, because then our servers get less shifts, less tips. … Our small businesses feel the impact too because their patrons are tightening their belts as well.”

Lee acknowledges that the policy has benefited her constituents. But she’d like to make it permanent and accessible to more people.

No taxes on tips reduces federal income tax up to $25,000 per year for workers who regularly receive tips, and it is set to expire at the end of 2028. It was expected to be a popular provision for Republicans to run on during the midterms. Both former Vice President Kamala Harris and Trump campaigned on eliminating taxes on tips in 2024, and it has bipartisan support.

Like much of the rest of the country, bigger economic factors are hitting this district. Last year, Las Vegas counted its lowest annual total visitors since 2021. Canadians, who make up the largest group of international travelers to Las Vegas, reduced their visits by about 17% last year as tensions over tariffs between the U.S. and Canada escalated. A “K-shaped” economy is also leading to top earners prospering as lower income households struggle to make ends meet.

“Every month I struggle to make the payments, and it's really hard for me as a mother,” Patricia Soto, a longtime Culinary Union member, said after handing out materials in support of Lee and other Democrats on the ballot in a neighborhood in Las Vegas. “We try everything that we can. So, for me, it's very bad right now. Very, very bad. We need a change. We really need a change about that.”

Given those broader trends, Republicans are struggling to frame the reconciliation bill around popular policies like no taxes on tips.

“That's been the Republicans' biggest problem is messaging and better explaining to the common man what it is that these things do, the policies that they're trying to enact,” Nate Poort, who works as a roadie in the entertainment industry, said at a Nevada Republican Club lunch in Las Vegas.

O’Donnell, who wrote music for the video game Halo and has never held elected office, is leaning into the policy and is not worried that the rest of the reconciliation package, whose popularity has remained low, will eclipse it. He has two more weeks to see if it can help his party flip the seat, even as a super PAC affiliated with MAGA Inc. has reportedly pulled back $1 million it planned to spend on his behalf.

The cuts to Medicaid and SNAP benefits tucked into the tax bill are efforts by Republicans to reduce federal spending, he argues, and the no-tax-on-tips provision has a bipartisan appeal in an economy where people want to be able to afford homes and basic costs.

O’Donnell’s philosophy is that most people live what he calls “conservative” lives.

“They get up in the morning, they go to work, they're trying to purchase a home or they have a home, and they're trying to educate their kids, and they're responsible. Things like no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security actually has an impact on their lives,” O’Donnell told The Sun. “I think that's the way most people live, regardless of what their political affiliation is.”

A new Politico poll found that tax cuts on tips and overtime pay was a top tax issue for voters but less important to them than increasing taxes for billionaires or ending tax breaks for large companies.

How persuasive no taxes on tips will ultimately be in the 3rd Congressional District is up to how each party frames no tax on tips and the reconciliation package it’s tucked into, said Amy Tarkanian, a former chair of the Nevada Republican Party.

“The way that he's relaying this message, it is in lockstep with President Trump,” she said of O’Donnell. “I think that's what you're probably seeing across the nation.”

Tarkanian added that she doesn’t think many voters know the provision is temporary.

“They just hear it. It sounds great. It sounds uplifting. It sounds promising, and you're locked in, right?” Tarkanian said. “But maybe you don't understand the nuts and bolts.”

Tarkanian said that if Lee can successfully explain the nuances of why she didn’t support this version of no taxes on tips, “that puts her in a much stronger position.”

Lee’s challenge is to explain why she voted down the reconciliation package that included the no-tax-on-tips provision, which the lawmaker doesn’t see as an insurmountable hurdle.

“When people look at the equity and what happened in that bill, they can understand why I voted against it,” Lee told The Sun.
entries.author: Christa Dutton
